ABSTRACT

AMPLIFICATION OF KEY CATABOLIC GENES AND BIOREMEDIATION POTENTIAL OF DIESEL-DEGRADING BACTERIA FROM DUMPSITES AND AUTOMOBILE WORKSHOPS

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author: Olowomofe, Temitayo Omotunde, Oluwole, Adeoye Olusola and Babalola Toyin Funmilola

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.01.2026.43.49

Diesel pollution remains a major environmental challenge, especially in areas where petroleum handling and waste management practices fall short of standards. This research investigated the biodegradation potential of bacteria isolated from automobile workshops and municipal dumpsites, with emphasis on amplifying key catabolic genes involved in hydrocarbon degradation. Six diesel-contaminated soil samples were collected and analysed for diesel-degrading microbes. Bacteria capable of using diesel as an energy source were isolated, purified, and characterized through morphological and biochemical tests and 16S rRNA sequencing. Both whole cells (cell pellets; CP) and cell-free extracts (CFE) were evaluated for degradation performance using gas chromatography. Total bacterial counts ranged from 2.50 ± 0.10 to 3.10 ± 0.05 Log CFU/g, while hydrocarbon-utilizing bacteria ranged from 1.80 ± 0.09 to 2.30 ± 0.05. Twenty-one isolates were obtained, with three highly efficient strains identified from dumpsite soil as Pseudomonas aeruginosa WLS4, Proteus penneri Rizhao_556_1, and Alcaligenes faecalis C5. These isolates carried multiple hydrocarbon-degrading genes (alkB1, PAH, and NAHAC). Their cell-free extracts showed higher degradation potential than whole cells, with TPH values of 0.4067, 0.4644, and 0.4333 compared to 0.6507, 0.593, and 0.5835 for CP treatments. The results indicate that extracellular enzymes in the extracts play a major role in hydrocarbon breakdown and may enhance remediation where bacterial growth is limited.
